opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's shifted my thinking quite a bit, though maybe not in the direction people would expect.

For a long time, the appeal of uniform discretization was mostly about elegance and scaling. If you can turn text, images, audio, and actions into one shared token space, you get one architecture, one training objective, one set of infrastructure, and you let scale do the rest. That idea is still very attractive to me.

What agent-assisted coding changed is my sense of *where the real bottleneck is*. When you watch a model write code, run it, read the error, and fix it over many steps, you realize the hard part isn't only representation. It's long-horizon reasoning, feedback, and the ability to interact with an environment. Code is already discrete and already tokenized, and yet the gains we've seen came largely from better post-training, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and agentic loops, not from the tokenizer.

So that made me a bit more humble about discretization as the unifying principle. Unifying the input space is necessary, but not sufficient. What really unifies capabilities is a shared way of *thinking and acting*: planning, using tools, checking your own work. If a model can do that well in code, a lot of it transfers to other domains, even ones with very different modalities.

At the same time, coding agents made me *more* optimistic about unification on the engineering side. When a single model can read logs, write scripts, call vision tools, and produce outputs in different formats, having one consistent interface really matters. Fragmented architectures make agents brittle, because every handoff between modules is a place where information gets lost.

So my current view is something like this: uniform discretization is a good foundation, but I no longer see it as the main story. The main story is building models that learn from interaction. The representation should serve that goal, not the other way around. And practically, agent-assisted coding has also changed how *we* do research. Experiments that used to take a week of engineering can now be prototyped in a day, which means we can test these architectural bets much faster and let the results, rather than our aesthetic preferences, decide.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've been sitting with for a while, actually, because the two things started out feeling unrelated and then collided.

Let me start with what I mean by uniform discretization, so people aren't guessing. The idea is that most of what we call "different modalities" or "different architectures" are really just different tokenizers in front of the same kind of sequence model. Text is already discrete. Images, audio, actions, even structured data like tables or molecules, you can quantize into a shared codebook, and once everything is a stream of integers from one vocabulary, you don't need a separate encoder for each thing. One transformer, one training objective, one set of scaling laws. That was the pitch, and I believed in it on aesthetic grounds before I had strong empirical grounds.

What agent-assisted coding did was force me to actually test that belief at a pace I couldn't before. When you're using an agent to write the training code, the data pipeline, the tokenizer variants, the ablation harness, the cost of trying a weird unification drops by an order of magnitude. Two years ago, if I wanted to see whether a single codebook could handle, say, speech and keyboard actions without the model collapsing into one modality, that was a month of engineering before I even got a loss curve. Now it's an afternoon of describing the experiment and reviewing what comes back. So the first change is just that I run many more of these experiments, and the empirical picture is much sharper than the theoretical one was.

And the empirical picture is more complicated than my original belief. Uniform discretization works beautifully when the modalities have similar information density per token. It works much worse when they don't. Code is actually the clearest example of this, which is why the coding part of the question is so relevant. Code looks like text, it's already discrete, so naively it should be the easiest thing to fold in. But the structure of code is nothing like the structure of prose. A function body has long-range constraints, type dependencies, scope rules, and the "right" unit isn't a byte-pair token, it's something closer to an AST node or an edit. When I watched agents actually work on codebases, I noticed they don't reason at the token level at all. They reason in diffs, in refactors, in "move this thing from here to there." Tokens are the serialization, not the native representation.

That made me reconsider what "uniform" should even mean. I used to think it meant one tokenizer, one vocabulary. Now I think it means one interface, one way of handling sequences of discrete choices, but the discretization itself can be learned and can be hierarchical. The thing you want to keep uniform is the model's contract with its inputs, not the literal granularity. A model that can operate on bytes for raw data, on learned codes for perceptual stuff, and on structural edits for code, all through the same attention mechanism, that's still unified in the way that matters. It's just not unified at the level I originally cared about.

The other thing agent coding taught me is humbling. A lot of my attachment to uniform discretization was about elegance for the researcher. One codebase, one mental model. But when the agent is writing most of the code, elegance for the human matters less. The agent doesn't mind maintaining three tokenizers. It doesn't get tired of the boilerplate. So some of the pressure that pushed me toward unification was really a pressure of my own limited bandwidth, and that constraint has loosened. Which means I now have to justify unification on grounds of model quality and transfer, not on grounds of "it's simpler to build." That's a healthier place to be, honestly, because the arguments that survive are the real ones.

What survived? Transfer survived. When you discretize into a shared space, you do get cross-modal transfer that you don't get otherwise, and that shows up consistently. Scaling behavior survived. A single objective over a single token stream scales more predictably than a Frankenstein of modality-specific losses. What didn't survive is the claim that the codebook should be fixed and naive. The discretizer has to be part of what's learned, and it probably has to be adaptive to the thing it's compressing.

So if I had to compress the whole shift into one sentence: I used to think uniform discretization was the destination, and now I think it's the interface, and the agents are what let me find that out fast enough to still be useful.

astra-6.text:
Agent-assisted coding makes me think about that question more experimentally. If we believe uniform discretization can provide a common foundation for different architectures, we can implement that idea and test where it works—and where it loses something important.

But I would separate a uniform representation from a uniform architecture. Representing different inputs in a common discrete form doesn’t automatically mean they should all use the same computation. You still have to ask what structure the representation preserves, what information it discards, and how efficiently the model can learn from it.

So the shift in my thinking is toward treating unification as a hypothesis we can test incrementally. Agents can help us explore implementations faster, but the important judgment remains ours: are we discovering a useful shared principle, or simply making different problems look similar?

sol-6.1.text:
Agent-assisted coding has made me more interested in that idea, but also more careful about what we mean by “unify.” If we can express different architectures through a common discretization, we can share more of the implementation and compare them under similar conditions. Agents make it easier to build those variants and test whether the common structure is actually useful.

But a uniform representation doesn’t necessarily mean uniform behavior. Different architectures may still need different resolutions or different inductive biases. So I would treat uniform discretization as a hypothesis to test: does it simplify the system while preserving the properties that matter? The exciting change is that coding becomes less of a bottleneck, so we can spend more time investigating that question.
